title: D-Wave QPU parameter ranges
text: On Advantage_system4: num_reads 1-10000; annealing_time 0.5-2000 microseconds, default 20; h_range [-4, 4], j_range [-1, 1] (extended_j_range [-2, 1]). With auto_scale (default on) the embedded Ising problem is rescaled into these ranges, so the QPU sees relative, not absolute, coefficient sizes.

title: D-Wave QPU cost model
text: Billing is QPU access time. It grows with num_reads (each read costs roughly annealing_time + readout + delay) plus a fixed programming overhead per call. Doubling num_reads roughly doubles sampling time; longer annealing_time also adds per-read time. P0 run: 100 reads at 20 us used about 25-28 ms of QPU access time for 8-variable problems.
source: Ocean timing fields; our P0 runs (verified)

title: D-Wave minor embedding and chains
text: Logical variables are embedded as chains of physical qubits. Ocean's EmbeddingComposite picks chain_strength with uniform torque compensation when it is not set, and resolves broken chains by majority vote. A dense QUBO (all pairs coupled, e.g. cardinality constraints) needs long chains as n grows. Chain breaks corrupt samples; a very large chain_strength instead dominates the auto-scaled coefficient range and squeezes the problem's own couplings.

title: Fujitsu Digital Annealer v3c interface
text: Async REST job: submit binary_polynomial terms with a fujitsuDA3 parameter block, poll the job, then DELETE it (finished jobs count against a job limit). The offset is not sent, so returned energies exclude it. Results list solutions with energy and frequency; timing.solve_time is in milliseconds. time_limit_sec is the main effort knob (each job ran about time_limit_sec of solve time in our runs). Quota: 300 minutes of DA time per month for this account, so every second of time_limit_sec counts.

title: Fujitsu DA3 search parameters
text: fujitsuDA3 parameters and limits measured on v3c: time_limit_sec integer >= 1 (non-integers rejected); num_output_solution 1-1024 (server default 5); num_run >= 1 (129 accepted); num_group 1-16; gs_level 0-100; gs_cutoff >= 0; unknown parameter names are rejected. More output solutions give the feedback extractor a better view of feasibility and diversity at no extra solve time.

title: Simulated annealing (dwave-samplers) parameters
text: num_reads = independent restarts; num_sweeps = Metropolis sweeps per restart (more sweeps = slower cooling, better equilibration). If beta_range is not given it is derived from the QUBO biases, so multiplying the whole QUBO by a constant has essentially no effect on SA. Penalty weights do change the landscape: very large penalties make the objective differences tiny relative to the temperature schedule.

title: CGA (Compal GPU Annealer)
text: Socket.IO API that accepts a QUBO dict, offset and timeout and returns a pickled sampleset plus run_time (unit not documented). Adapter not implemented until the API and its tunable parameters are confirmed.

title: Fujitsu DA job behaviour (operational)
text: Submission always returns HTTP 200; invalid parameters only appear when the job runs, as status 'Error' with a message such as 'num_group must be <= 16'. A running job cannot be cancelled or deleted: it runs until its time limit, so a mistaken large time_limit_sec costs that much solver time. Error and Done jobs can be deleted.

title: Measured: same QUBOs on SA, Fujitsu DA and D-Wave
text: Default settings, one run each, 2026-10-04. Dense select_k n=30 k=6 (optimum 110): SA (100 reads, 1000 sweeps) 87% feasible, optimum found; Fujitsu DA (time_limit_sec=1) 100% feasible, optimum found, mean feasible 108.2; D-Wave Advantage_system4 (100 reads, default chain strength) 1% feasible, best 81 (gap 26%) because of chain breaks. Knapsack n=14 with binary slack (20 variables, coefficient dynamic range 320, optimum 170): SA 98% feasible, best 159 (gap 6.5%); Fujitsu DA (1 s) 100% feasible, optimum found. Fujitsu handled both dense couplings and the large dynamic range without tuning; D-Wave needs chain_strength and penalty tuning first on dense problems.
source: our runs via scripts/run_backend.py and exp_dwave_chain_strength.py, 2026-10-04 (single runs)

title: D-Wave: trading annealing time against number of reads
text: Request many read-anneal cycles; returns diminish roughly logarithmically. Balancing annealing time and readout time is described as cost-effective. In D-Wave's own example, moving from 10,000 reads at 1 us to 1,000 reads at 50 us raised the yield of best solutions from 1.31% to 4.0%. The best split under a fixed time budget is problem-dependent and must be found by experiment.
source: D-Wave docs, QPU Configuration: Best Practices (docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_configuration.html), read 2026-10-04

title: D-Wave: auto_scale and dynamic range
text: With auto_scale (default on) biases are rescaled to use the full h/J range. A single outsized coefficient can squash the usable range for all others (D-Wave cites factors of 25 or more), so large penalty weights or a large chain_strength reduce the effective precision of the objective terms. Large individual biases can be split across several chained qubits to reduce precision demands.
source: D-Wave docs, QPU Configuration: Best Practices (docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_configuration.html), read 2026-10-04

title: D-Wave: spin-reversal transforms and post-processing
text: Spin-reversal (gauge) transforms reduce systematic biases from QPU imperfections without changing the problem; Ocean's SpinReversalTransformComposite applies several, at a multiple of the runtime. Default embedding composites repair broken chains (majority vote), and a classical local search (e.g. SteepestDescentSolver) can polish QPU samples. Not yet exposed in our adapter's action space.
source: D-Wave docs, QPU Configuration: Best Practices (docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_configuration.html), read 2026-10-04

title: D-Wave: anneal schedule controls (pauses, reverse annealing, anneal offsets)
text: Pauses near the region where the problem freezes, reverse annealing from a good classical solution (quantum-assisted local search), and per-qubit anneal offsets can raise ground-state probability sharply on specific problems (D-Wave's examples report large gains). These are advanced, problem-specific controls; our adapter does not expose them yet.
source: D-Wave docs, QPU Configuration: Best Practices (docs.dwavequantum.com/en/latest/quantum_research/solver_configuration.html), read 2026-10-04

title: Fujitsu DA user guide: precision and job limits
text: FujitsuDA3Solver handles up to 100,000 bits; quadratic coefficients are 64-bit signed integers and linear coefficients 76-bit, so coefficient dynamic range is rarely the limiting factor on DA (consistent with our knapsack run). Up to 16 concurrent asynchronous requests and up to 16 stored jobs. The request format also has a separate penalty polynomial field (penalty_binary_polynomial), worth checking against the API reference before use.
source: Fujitsu Computing as a Service Digital Annealer User's Guide, 8th ed. (portal.aispf.global.fujitsu.com/apidoc/da/jp/da-guide-en.html), read 2026-10-04
